question.prompt:
\(ABC\) and \(A'B'C'\) are equilateral triangles with parallel sides and the same center, as in the figure. The distance between side \(BC\) and side \(B'C'\) is \(\frac16\) the altitude of \(\triangle ABC.\) The ratio of the area of \(\triangle A'B'C'\) to the area of \(\triangle ABC\) is

[Figure 1](figures/1988_AMC_12_Q16_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The center of an equilateral triangle lies one-third of its altitude above any side. This follows because its altitudes are also medians, and the centroid divides each median in the ratio \(2:1\), measured from the vertex. This lets us convert the given gap between bases into a ratio of altitudes.

The supplied figure shows \(A'B'C'\) inside \(ABC\), with the same orientation and with \(B'C'\) between \(BC\) and their common center.

Let \(h>0\) be the altitude of \(ABC\), and let \(h'>0\) be the altitude of \(A'B'C'\). Their common center is \(h/3\) above \(BC\). Since \(B'C'\) is \(h/6\) above \(BC\), the center is
\[
\frac h3-\frac h6=\frac h6
\]
above \(B'C'\). Applying the same center-to-base relation to the smaller triangle gives
\[
\frac{h'}3=\frac h6,
\qquad h'=\frac h2.
\]
All equilateral triangles are similar, and their area ratio is the square of their altitude ratio. Hence
\[
\frac{[A'B'C']}{[ABC]}=\left(\frac{h'}h\right)^2=\left(\frac12\right)^2=\boxed{\frac14},
\]
where brackets denote area. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Use the center's position on an altitude

solutions.explanation:
We can find the center's distance from a side directly from triangle areas. In an equilateral triangle, the center lies on all three angle bisectors, so its perpendicular distances to the three sides are equal. Join the center to the three vertices. This splits the triangle into three triangles with equal bases and equal heights.

Let the outer triangle have side length \(a>0\), altitude \(h>0\), and center-to-side distance \(r\). Computing its area first as one triangle and then as three triangles gives
\[
\frac12 ah=3\left(\frac12 ar\right),
\qquad r=\frac h3.
\]
The same argument shows that the smaller triangle's center-to-side distance \(r'\) equals one-third of its altitude \(h'\).

The supplied figure shows the smaller base between the outer base and the common center. Therefore the given base separation implies
\[
r'=r-\frac h6=\frac h3-\frac h6=\frac h6.
\]
Thus \(h'=3r'=h/2\). The two equilateral triangles are similar, so their side lengths also have ratio \(1/2\). Using base times height divided by two, their area ratio is
\[
\frac{[A'B'C']}{[ABC]}=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\boxed{\frac14}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
